paragraphs: When Fu Jian reached the western camp, the commander’s banner hung halfway down its pole. Two guards saluted together at the gate, a Di man from Guanzhong and a Xianbei from Hebei. Their accents were worlds apart; their hands moved in the same pattern laid down by the new army regulations. Beyond them, spent medicinal herbs lay warm in a charcoal brazier. A clerk had hung a rain-soaked military map beside the coals to dry. Red circles crowded the bends of the Fei River.

Murong Chui sat behind his desk with a thick fur cloak wrapped tightly around his shoulders. His armor lay by his pillow; its plates had been mended many times. The familiar bronze paperweight still held down a corner of the map. Hearing footsteps, he merely said, “The man on the southern bank did not surrender the cities.”
“You have not risen from bed all day. How do you know what happened aboard the boat?”
“If the talks had succeeded, Your Majesty would be sending orders to the armies by now, not coming to listen to a sick man.”

Fu Jian sat opposite him. Fu Rong ordered an attendant to bring a brazier, but Murong Chui waved it away. The smell of medicine was thick in the tent, and the fire already burned too fiercely. He asked to see the original agreement from the river meeting and turned its pages one by one. At the provisions permitting soldiers and civilians to travel between the sides, he stopped and asked whether Jin merchants could still trade salt and cloth along the route. When assured they could, he scratched a small mark in the margin with his fingernail.
“Even merchants have your attention now, General,” Fu Jian said.

“Our army stands here because its supply roads stand,” Murong Chui said quietly. “Seal every civilian boat as soon as war begins, and even the government vessels will have nowhere to hire oarsmen. Besides, traders travel the river. Ask them where the channels run deep or where bandits wait, and you will learn faster than by asking officers.”

A few sentences brought on a fit of coughing that shook his chest. An attendant held out a bronze basin. He covered his mouth with his sleeve; when he lowered his hand, the cuff was stained a dark red. Fu Jian reached to take the military map away, but Murong Chui put a hand over it and laughed. “So many things have been taken from me in this life. Now I cannot bear to lose even a map.”
Fu Jian did not smile. He rested a hand gently on the paper. “Fu Rong can command today. You should rest.”

“The Duke of Yangping can attack, and he can hold a position,” Murong Chui said. “But the Jiang–Huai region will breed a new kind of enemy. Liu Yu started with neither inheritance nor patron to rely on. He gathered men through victories. Why would he let our army array itself on a broad official road and fight a pitched battle? He will burn a storehouse, seize a narrow channel, lead cavalry into a mudflat, and strike elsewhere. If you judge only the victories and defeats of a single day, sooner or later you will find yourself chasing the stern of his boat.”

Fu Rong stepped forward and opened another terrain map. The marshlands south of the Yellow River were washed in pale ink, and Murong Chui had annotated every navigable waterway in a tiny hand. Only three places were ringed in bright vermilion, each marked as dangerous to enter. Fu Rong asked whether they should build more large ships near the mouth of the Huai. Murong Chui shook his head. Large ships could hold a main river, not work their way through narrow inlets. Qin sailors would need southerners who knew the waters of Wu and Yue; their earlier household registrations must not be used as an excuse to employ them only as grain porters.
“Can surrendered soldiers be trusted?” Fu Rong asked.

“If you treat their sons and daughters as Qin subjects but refuse to let them touch the helm, whom are you asking them to trust?” Murong Chui kept one finger on a thin blue channel. “There are patrols for catching spies. That is different from treating an entire camp as spies. If you want these men to march a long road beside you, first let them earn a place at your side.”

The words were scarcely out when he suddenly could not draw breath. He collapsed forward, both arms braced on the desk, and the bronze paperweight struck the floor. Fu Jian rose to support him while Fu Rong called for the physician. The doctor pressed a thick hot cloth to the old general’s chest and tried to force medicine down his throat. Murong Chui stopped him with an upraised hand and swallowed only a few mouthfuls of warm water. Nearly eighty years old, his once iron frame was like a beam weathered by years of snow: upright to the eye, but threaded within by invisible cracks and rot.

The physician asked both visitors to withdraw. Fu Jian stayed where he was and ordered him to speak plainly about the illness. Prostrate on the floor, the doctor said the disease of the lungs had deepened, that the general might soon be unable to rise, and that no one could yet tell whether he would survive the winter. Murong Chui heard everything from his bed. When the doctor had left, he asked, “Your Majesty was once most afraid I might keep a second allegiance. Are you still afraid?”
Fu Rong raised his head. Fu Jian picked up the fallen bronze paperweight, set it back on the desk, and answered calmly, “I was.”
“Wang Jinglüe said I could not be trusted.”
“He had his reasons.”

Murong Chui gazed at the roof of the tent. After a long silence, he said, “He was not wrong. After Wang Meng died, I thought of Yan every day. I kept memories of the bell tower at Ye, the old banners north of Ji, and even notes sent by former ministers. Your Majesty entrusted me with armies. After every victory I wondered: if I led my soldiers away now, might there not still be men in Hebei willing to follow?”
Ash settled in the brazier, revealing a single dark-red ember. Fu Rong silently rolled up half the military map.
“Why did you never go?” Fu Jian asked.

“At first, because I could not. Later, because there was no road back.” Murong Chui closed his eyes for a moment. “In the year of the great flood at Ye, I met many former ministers of Yan. They brought seals from the old palace to invite me, laid on a feast, sang Yan songs, and said that if I called from a high place the days since our kingdom fell might all be undone. But outside the banquet children went hungry. The old families had hidden millet upstairs, waiting to draw relief from Qin granaries when they opened. Suddenly I no longer recognized the men at that table.”
“They were your old companions.”

“That is precisely why they were so hard to see through. Some wanted Yan restored for the land and people they remembered. Others wanted their old soldiers and fields, or a mansion already sheltering flood victims. If I raised the Yan banner, all of them could gather beneath it. On the road back to Ye, it would still be children who had never known Yan whose blood was spilled.”

Fu Jian studied the gaunt hand before him and suddenly recalled their first meeting in Chang’an many years before. Murong Chui’s armor had still carried dust from Yan, and he had spoken cautiously, yet his eyes held an old country that no one could take from him. That look had not gone out; it had merely drawn farther inward. He had never forgotten Former Yan, nor had he ever made forgetfulness the proof of his loyalty.
“If you lived longer, you might still regret your choice,” Fu Jian said.
Murong Chui nodded slowly. “I would. When dreams return at dusk, I fear hearing an old Yan song, then waking to find even the singers gone.”

Fu Rong glanced toward the two shadows of guards on the entrance curtain and asked whether the old Yan companies might stir now that the general was gravely ill. Murong Chui summoned his military secretary and delivered to Fu Rong, one by one, the roster of camp commanders, duplicate tiger-tally vouchers, and the granary key tokens. From the next day forward, the camps were to answer roll call according to central command’s existing orders. No one might alter a deployment privately because the commander was ill. The secretary was a man of Yan, and his eyes reddened as he received the instructions, but he still repeated the camp numbers and order of units as regulations required.

“In former days, if I fell, the first question in camp would have been who should carry the Murong banner in my place,” Murong Chui murmured. “If all you ask tomorrow is where the grain for the following day will come from, that will be a good thing.”

At dusk the watch drums sounded outside. Two men registered from distant regions quarreled over the hour for changing sentries. One spoke in the Guanzhong dialect, the other cursed back in Xianbei. The secretary summoned them, checked the duty book, and sentenced them both to two shifts at the camp gate. He asked neither man’s tribe. Murong Chui listened for a long time and at last smiled. “Fighting men do not learn proper ways all at once.”

After nightfall Fu Jian dismissed his attendants, leaving only Fu Rong with him. Murong Chui spoke of two matters to be settled after his death. First, former Yan soldiers were not to be compelled to observe mourning for him, nor were the camps to be divided once more by ethnicity under the pretext of honoring their commander. Second, he did not wish to return to the ancestral Murong tombs at Ye, or to lie beside the graves of the Fu imperial clan. They should find a slope at the western foot of the Taihang Mountains, beside the courier road leading to Guanzhong, from which the distant peaks could be seen and eastbound and westbound travelers could pass nearby. The inscription should say only “Murong Chui,” with neither “King of Yan” nor “Surrendered Minister” added.
“You are sparing me the debate over your posthumous title,” Fu Jian said, forcing a smile.

“No matter how sharp the historians' brushes, they cannot change the life I have lived.” Murong Chui regarded him for a while. “I fought for Yan once, and later I fought for Qin. I killed men on both sides. The stone need not declare either side the best.”
“And if your children or grandchildren wish to go back to Ye and tend the family tombs?”
“Let the living choose their own roads.”
Fu Jian was silent for a long time. Then Murong Chui pointed once more at the map. “One more thing must not be buried with me.”

He showed Fu Rong the three waterways by which Liu Yu might attack, marking a note beside an old granary: the ditch must actually be dug, the fire-fighting equipment actually inspected; a clerk’s report that all was prepared was not enough. His strokes were wavering, one nearly illegible. Fu Rong bent to decipher it, and Murong Chui took his wrist and guided the brush over the words again.
“What if Liu Yu refuses to submit?” Fu Jian asked.

“Then fight him,” Murong Chui said. “When I was young, I too feared that men would say I dared not take a city. Once I had taken it, the people had often burned down their own homes. If Your Majesty hopes the south will come over to Qin, do not return its cities to the people with nothing left but broken walls.”
“You wish me to spare Liu Yu.”

“If you meet him in battle and he must be killed, kill him.” Murong Chui’s voice grew faint. “But if, in order to kill him, you destroy the villages and towns he seeks to protect, what will Your Majesty have left when you win?”

The following day the old general rallied a little, drank half a bowl of rice gruel, and sent his map to the central command. On the third day fever came. He drifted between waking and delirium. An old officer who had served him since Ye arrived at the tent, burst into tears, and fell to his knees crying, “My king!” Murong Chui opened his eyes only after a long while. “There is no king in this army. Go and muster the men.”

The old officer would not rise. It was the military secretary, himself Xianbei, who helped him out. Outside the tent roll call began. Each man held a roster, and together they checked every absence, camp by camp, until the last soldier had answered. After they dispersed, Murong Chui asked which camp’s drum he had heard, then whether snow had fallen yet in Yan. His attendant did not know. He gently spread the old fur cloak over him.

Rain fell through the night, from midnight nearly until dawn. The guards outside heard the patient’s breathing grow weaker behind the curtain and summoned the physician. Several men stood around the bed, but by the end of the hour of the Tiger no sound remained. When the morning drum sounded, Murong Chui’s hand lay outside the blanket, two fingers slightly curled, their tips pressed against the mattress. The physician reached out to test for life, then slowly covered the hand again.

The news reached central command while Fu Jian was examining a memorial about grain transport. The messenger gave the name and said that the general had died during the hour of the Tiger. Fu Jian sat holding his brush, unable for a long time to write a character. The commanders before his desk waited for a ruling on the grain allotment. At last he wrote “Postpone for now,” returned the memorial, and ordered a half-day suspension of drills. No one was to assemble a faction at the bier, cause trouble, or raise the banners of a former kingdom without authorization.

Fu Rong asked how the funeral should be conducted. Qin ceremonial law, Yan rites, and the different traditions of the army all contradicted one another in places. Fu Jian listened, then said, “Bury him with the honors due a general of the realm. Let those who accompany him weep in the speech of their own homes. There is no need to teach everyone the same way of mourning.”

Soldiers lined the route from the western camp to the post road. At the front stood veteran Xianbei, their faces crossed by scars; many had defended the cities of Yan for the Murong clan. Behind them came Di soldiers, Qiang archers, Han infantrymen, and units of Dingling and Xiongnu. Their armor differed, but their banners bore the same system of unit numbers. The two gate guards took their prescribed places before the bier, one holding the right shaft, the other steadying the left yoke. No one told them to exchange places when the coffin passed through the gate.

A white-haired former Yan minister drew from his sleeve an old banner folded into a tiny square. He hesitated for a long time and did not unfold it. The corner of red that showed disappeared back into his sleeve. He retreated into the funeral crowd. Fu Jian saw him but never asked his name, even after the procession had dispersed.

The coffin traveled west, passing several relay stations in Henei before halting where the Taihang Mountains began to fall away. The slope was hard earth and broken stone; the grave diggers worked for two days. In accordance with Murong Chui’s wishes, his descendants raised neither stone beasts nor a lofty mound, only a plain blue-gray stele. As the mason cut the third character, a corner of his chisel broke off and left a fine crack across the stroke. He offered to replace the stone, but Fu Jian said there was no need; the cut could be smoothed as it stood.

When the stele was set upright, a convoy of salt wagons happened to be passing westward below the slope. Seeing soldiers gathered by the road, a driver checked his horses. Told that an old Qin general was being buried there, he asked whether he should take another road. The guards shook their heads and waved him through. Wheels went around the foot of the hill, leaving two shallow ruts. Murong Chui had wanted a grave beside a road; the road, sure enough, remained open to travelers.

Only after the troops had withdrawn did Fu Rong bring forward the final roll-call register. The former troops of Murong Chui remained on duty under the new army’s orders. A handful of old retainers had sought leave to return home, but no unit called itself an army of Yan and no one had raised another commander. Turning the pages of names written side by side, Fu Jian saw that the two young guards had been assigned the first watch after the funeral. Those men had stood outside the general’s tent for days. Now they stood together at the relay road, each reaching over to straighten the other’s helmet tassel where the wind had blown it askew.
Fu Jian looked toward the gravestone. “If Jinglüe were here and saw this day, I wonder what he would say.”
Fu Rong looked down at the soldiers on the hillside but did not presume to answer for Wang Meng.

On the return journey to the Fei River, Fu Jian said nothing more about the former Yan. At dusk he told Fu Rong to hang the old general’s waterway map beside the imperial desk and sent men to inspect every granary ditch circled on it. Actual dimensions, the number of fire-fighting implements, and full lists of guards were to be reported; the words “All prepared” would not suffice. He also ordered the vanguard to wait for formal orders before crossing any water. No one was to use the general’s death as a reason to rush into battle.

At the relay station, lamps were lit. Fu Jian pulled off his wet boots and found a small stone from the burial slope caught in one sole. He laid it beside the lamp, intending to carry it back to the Fei the next day. Gray-white, no larger than a pebble left after repairs to the old palace walls in Chang’an. His lamp burned far into the night. On the map, river after river still ran south.
